# Long-Wagner Conjecture 5.1: cube-free subsets of Z/2^nZ have density at most 5/8


Call $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ *cube-free* if no triple $x, y, z$ has all seven of $x$, $y$, $z$, $x+y$, $y+z$, $z+x$, $x+y+z$ inside $A$. The triple is unconstrained, so a degenerate one counts. Write $f(n)$ for the largest size of a cube-free subset.

The conjecture is that $f(n) \le \frac{5}{8} 2^n$ for every $n$.

This is Conjecture 5.1 of Jason Long and Adam Zsolt Wagner, *The largest projective cube-free subsets of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$*, [arXiv:1810.01225](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.01225). It has been open since October 2018, and a 2026 journal paper still names it as conjectured: Yuchen Meng, *On Cube-Free Problems*, Electron. J. Combin. 33(1) (2026) #P1.16.

## The constant is attained

The bound is sharp, and the extremal set is explicit: $A = \{v : v \bmod 8 \in \{1,3,4,5,7\}\}$, the odd residues together with those congruent to 4 mod 8. Its size is $2^{n-1} + 2^{n-3} = \frac{5}{8} 2^n$. In the layer language of Long and Wagner this is $C_3 = L_1 \cup L_3$.

## What is known

The conjecture holds for unions of layers. That is Long-Wagner Theorem 1.10 at $d = 3$, and it is the largest class on which the conjectured constant is proved.

For arbitrary sets the best published unconditional bound is $f(n) < \frac{2}{3} 2^n$. Meng calls this bound "quite trivial" and gives it in one paragraph for every cyclic group, so it should not be read as progress toward $5/8$. The residual gap is exactly $\frac{2}{3} - \frac{5}{8} = \frac{1}{24}$, that is $2^n/24$ elements.

Small values are $f(1) = 1$, $f(2) = 2$, $f(3) = 5$, $f(4) = 10$, $f(5) = 20$, $f(6) = 40$, $f(7) = 80$, matching $2^{n-1} + 2^{n-3}$ from $n = 3$ on.

Those seven values come from solver searches rather than from proofs, Gurobi in Long and Wagner for $n \le 7$ together with an independent SAT reproduction here, and the two halves of the claim are not on the same footing. The SAT half that matters, the unsatisfiability of "a cube-free set of size 81 exists at $n = 7$", is a solver claim backed by neither a checked proof certificate nor a kernel check. The witness half is verified: a set of exactly 80 elements was produced and re-checked cube-free. So $f(7) \ge 80$ is solid and $f(7) \le 80$ is not certified. No part of this mission rests on either.

## What the items are

The goal item is the open conjecture itself, for $n \ge 4$. Every other item is a milestone that is proved mathematics. The two closed instances $n = 4$ and $n = 5$ are stated separately because they are the only cases of the goal that a proof assistant has actually settled here.

The chain runs: the base case mod 8 by exhaustion, monotonicity under subsets, the bridge between the membership form and the `Finset` form of the forbidden configuration, sharpness, the odd-residue tight case, the layer-union theorem, the two-thirds bound, and then $n = 4$ and $n = 5$.

## Notes on the formalization

Six definitions live in one definition item, `Def_Z2nCubeFreeLayers`: `HasCube`, `CubeFree`, `config`, `ConfigFree`, `layerIdx` and `IsLayerUnion`. `layerIdx` is written through the 2-adic valuation rather than through a congruence, because the congruence form leaves $0$ in no layer at all and needs the last layer special-cased.

`CubeFree` and `ConfigFree` are two encodings of the same condition and they are not definitionally equal, because `config` collapses duplicates on a degenerate triple. Their equivalence is a milestone rather than an assumption.

## Cube-free sets and layers in $\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$


The six definitions the Long-Wagner cube-free mission is stated in.

`HasCube A` says some triple $x, y, z$, not required distinct, has all seven of $x$, $y$, $z$, $x+y$, $y+z$, $z+x$, $x+y+z$ inside $A$. `CubeFree A` is its negation.

`config x y z` is the same seven elements as a `Finset`, which collapses duplicates on a degenerate triple, and `ConfigFree A` says no `config` is a subset of $A$. The equivalence of the two encodings is a milestone of the mission, not an assumption of it.

`layerIdx n x` is the layer of $x$ in the Long-Wagner partition of $\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$: layer $i$ for $1 \le i \le n$ is the residues congruent to $2^{i-1}$ mod $2^i$, and layer $n+1$ is $\{0\}$. It is defined through the 2-adic valuation rather than through a congruence, because the congruence form leaves $0$ in no layer at all. `IsLayerUnion n A` says $A$ contains a whole layer whenever it contains one element of it.

## Long-Wagner Conjecture 5.1: a cube-free set mod $2^n$ has size at most $\frac{5}{8}2^n$


For every $n \ge 4$ and every $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ that avoids every configuration $\{x, y, z, x+y, y+z, z+x, x+y+z\}$, we have $8|A| \le 5 \cdot 2^n$, that is $|A| \le \frac{5}{8}2^n$.

This statement is open. It is Conjecture 5.1 of Long and Wagner, stated in October 2018 and still named as conjectured in a 2026 journal paper.

The triple $x, y, z$ is unconstrained, so a degenerate triple counts and the condition is genuinely about affine 3-cubes rather than about distinct generators. The constant is attained by $\{v : v \bmod 8 \in \{1,3,4,5,7\}\}$, so it cannot be improved.

## The conjecture at $n = 5$


A cube-free $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/32\mathbb{Z}$ satisfies $8|A| \le 5 \cdot 32$, that is $|A| \le 20$.

Unlike $n = 4$, counting is not enough here. The two-thirds bound gives $|A| \le 21$, and the last element has to be excluded by a structural argument about which residues can coexist.

## The conjecture at $n = 4$


A cube-free $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/16\mathbb{Z}$ satisfies $8|A| \le 5 \cdot 16$, that is $|A| \le 10$.

The two constants differ at $n = 4$ but the integer maxima they admit coincide: $\frac{2}{3} \cdot 16 = 10.67$ and $\frac{5}{8} \cdot 16 = 10$, and the two-thirds bound already forces $|A| \le 10$. So this instance of the conjecture follows from the unconditional bound.

## The unconditional two-thirds bound


For every $n$, a cube-free $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ satisfies $3|A| + 1 \le 2^{n+1}$, so $|A| < \frac{2}{3}2^n$.

This bound should not be read as progress toward $\frac{5}{8}$, though it is the best unconditional constant available. Meng calls the two-thirds bound "quite trivial" and proves it in one paragraph for every cyclic group, not just for $\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$.

The residual gap is exactly $\frac{2}{3} - \frac{5}{8} = \frac{1}{24}$, so $2^n/24$ elements separate this from the conjecture.

## The tight case: a cube-free set containing every odd residue


Let $8 \mid N$ and let $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ be cube-free and contain every residue of odd value. Then $8|A| \le 5N$.

This is the case where the conjecture is tightest: a cube-free set that already contains all $N/2$ odd residues cannot beat the construction by adding even ones, and the bound says exactly how many even residues it may add.

## The two encodings of the forbidden configuration agree


For a finite subset $A$ of an additive abelian group, $A$ has a cube exactly when some `config x y z` is a subset of $A$.

`HasCube` lists the seven memberships separately; `config x y z` collects the same seven elements into a `Finset` and asks for a subset. The two are **not** definitionally equal, because the `Finset` collapses duplicates when the triple is degenerate: at $x = y = z = 1$ modulo 16 the configuration has three elements, not seven.

The claim is that deduplication leaves the equivalence intact, because subset of a `Finset` literal is the conjunction of the memberships either way.

## Long-Wagner Theorem 1.10 at $d = 3$: the conjecture holds for unions of layers


For every $n \ge 4$, a cube-free $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ that is a union of layers satisfies $8|A| \le 5 \cdot 2^n$.

The layers partition $\mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ by 2-adic valuation: layer $i$ for $1 \le i \le n$ is the residues congruent to $2^{i-1}$ mod $2^i$, and layer $n+1$ is $\{0\}$. `IsLayerUnion` says that containing one element of a layer means containing all of it.

This is the largest class on which the conjectured constant is proved. The extremal set $L_1 \cup L_3$ lies in the class, so the restriction keeps the sharpness.

## The base case: a cube-free subset of $\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$ has at most five elements


Every cube-free $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$ has $|A| \le 5$.

A finite check over all $2^8 = 256$ subsets. The bound is attained by $\{1, 3, 4, 5, 7\}$, which is the mod-8 shadow of the extremal construction, so it is sharp and not slack.

## Cube-freeness passes to subsets


If $B \subseteq A$ and $A$ is cube-free, then $B$ is cube-free.

Immediate from the definition, and needed by any induction that restricts the set to a coset or a subgroup.

## Sharpness: the constant $\frac{5}{8}$ is attained for every $n \ge 3$


For every $n \ge 3$ there is a cube-free $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ with $8|A| = 5 \cdot 2^n$ exactly.

The witness is $\{v : v \bmod 8 \in \{1,3,4,5,7\}\}$, the odd residues together with those congruent to 4 mod 8, of size $2^{n-1} + 2^{n-3}$. In Long and Wagner's layer notation this is $C_3 = L_1 \cup L_3$.

This is what makes the conjecture a conjecture about a sharp constant rather than about some constant.

## Base case: $f(3) = 5$ by exhaustion mod 8


A cube-free subset of $\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$ has at most five elements. The proof checks each of the 256 subsets. The constant $\frac{5}{8}$ enters here: the extremal set $\{1,3,4,5,7\}$ is the mod-8 shadow of the construction that attains the bound at every $n$.

## Cube-freeness passes to subsets


A subset of a cube-free set is cube-free. Short, and needed by every induction that restricts the set to a coset or a subgroup.

## The membership form and the Finset form of a cube agree


`HasCube` lists seven memberships and `config` collects the same seven elements into a `Finset`. They are not definitionally equal, because the `Finset` deduplicates: at the triple $(1,1,1)$ mod 16 the configuration has three elements. The milestone is that the equivalence holds despite the deduplication. A counting argument can then switch between the two forms freely.

## Sharpness: $\frac{5}{8}$ is attained for every $n \ge 3$


Exhibit a cube-free set of size exactly $\frac{5}{8}2^n$. The witness is $\{v : v \bmod 8 \in \{1,3,4,5,7\}\}$, of size $2^{n-1} + 2^{n-3}$. Without this the conjecture would be about some constant rather than about a sharp one, and a proof of any bound above $\frac{5}{8}$ could not be called close.

## The tight case: a set already containing every odd residue


For $8 \mid N$, a cube-free set containing all the odd residues of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ satisfies $8|A| \le 5N$. This is the configuration the extremal construction sits in, so it is where the bound is tightest and where any proof of the full conjecture has to be exact rather than generous.

## Long-Wagner Theorem 1.10: the conjecture for unions of layers


The conjectured bound, proved on the class of sets that contain a whole layer whenever they contain one element of it. This is proved mathematics and the largest class the constant is known on. The extremal set is itself a union of layers, so the restricted statement keeps the sharpness of the full one.

## The unconditional two-thirds bound and its limits


Every cube-free set satisfies $3|A| + 1 \le 2^{n+1}$. Include it because it is the best unconditional constant and because the two closed instances rest on it, and read it with the caveat Meng attaches: the bound is "quite trivial" and holds in every cyclic group. The slack against the conjecture is exactly $\frac{1}{24}$ of the group, so closing it is the whole remaining problem rather than a last step.

## The conjecture at $n = 4$


Counting suffices here. The two-thirds bound gives $|A| \le 10$ at $n = 4$, and $\frac{5}{8} \cdot 16 = 10$, so the two constants admit the same integer maximum and the instance falls out.

## The conjecture at $n = 5$, where counting stops working


The two-thirds bound gives $|A| \le 21$ and the conjecture asks for $|A| \le 20$, so one element has to be excluded by a structural argument about which residues can coexist. This is the smallest case that shows what a proof of the general conjecture would have to supply.
